extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and participants reading solutions to the Putnam Mathematical Competition (Putnam contestants, problem solvers)
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed solution writeups to Putnam competition problems (proof-based undergraduate-level contest problems). The page demonstrates techniques and structural criteria for producing correct, complete solutions to contest math problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symmetry to reduce cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit symmetry of the problem to reduce the number of cases to consider (e.g., in A1: 'Since the graph of y = f(x) is symmetric under reflection in the y-axis, it suffices to consider the case a ≥ 0').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the symmetry and justify restricting attention to a representative region or parameter sign; mention how the symmetric cases map back to original via reflection or sign change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem to guarantee existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the intermediate value theorem to show existence of solutions/ intersections when functions change sign (A1: to show any line must intersect the curve at least once).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show sign change or limit behavior at ±∞ (or endpoints) then invoke the theorem; include limits for x → ±∞ or evaluations at convenient points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Mean Value Theorem to bound number of intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the mean value theorem together with bounds on derivatives to show there cannot be multiple intersections (A1: if f′(x) < a then line and curve intersect at most once).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare slopes/derivatives; argue that if two intersections existed then mean value theorem would force derivative to equal a forbidden value; cite continuity and locations of equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze derivatives and critical points to count roots/intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: Study f′, its monotonicity and critical points and form g(x)=f(x)−ax to deduce number of solutions of g(x)=b (A1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute where derivative equals given parameter, identify maxima/minima of g, determine monotonicity intervals, and compare values g(r−), g(r+) to classify 0,1,2,3 intersections; provide explicit expressions for critical points when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit case analysis separating parameter regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the problem into natural parameter regimes (e.g., a = 0, |a| ≥ 1, 0 < |a| < 1) and treat each with tailored arguments (A1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each regime give existence/nonexistence or count statements and justify via prior tools (symmetry, derivatives, IVT/MVT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate coefficients of polynomial square and reason about signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Write p(x)=∑ a_i x^i, expand p(x)^2 = ∑ b_j x^j and use relationships like b1 = 2 a0 a1, b_{2n-1}=2 a_{n-1} a_n to bound how many coefficients can be negative (A2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate negativity of coefficients into sign conditions on the a_i, use elementary algebraic identities, and deduce impossibility via contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use induction on coefficients to propagate sign information
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume negativity pattern for some b_i and inductively deduce signs of a_i (A2 induction that ai<0 for i=1..n), reaching contradiction with a boundary coefficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State base case clearly, derive recurrence/inequality relating next coefficient, and complete induction; show final contradiction (e.g., b_{2n-1}>0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit example to show bound is sharp
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibit an explicit polynomial p(x) whose square attains the maximal number of negative coefficients to prove sharpness (A2 gives a specific p(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give explicit formula and expand or estimate coefficients to verify sign pattern; use bounding arguments on contributions from different terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce recurrence sequences to periodic behavior in finite fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify recurrence relations over finite fields and use algebraic manipulation to show periodicity and count admissible initial configurations (A3: recurrence an+2=(1+an+1)/an gives period 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute a few terms to detect period, state constraints on initial values to avoid division by zero, and count allowable initial pairs accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count objects via orbit decomposition under group action
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a cyclic permutation (periodic shift) action on tuples to partition sequences into orbits and count them modulo orbit sizes (A3 second solution: 5-periodic action divides S into orbits of size 1 or 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify stabilizers (constant tuples) and apply orbit-stabilizer style counting to deduce total count modulo period; separate fixed-point cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discriminant/residue considerations to count polynomial roots mod p
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate number of constant admissible sequences to roots of a quadratic and use discriminant/residue mod p to determine whether 0,2 roots occur (A3: discriminant 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute discriminant, state whether it is quadratic residue modulo p, and conclude the count of roots accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of expectation and independence to evaluate infinite sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend finite sums to infinite by zero-padding and compute expected value by summing expectations of individual summands using independence (A4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express event probabilities in terms of simpler independent events, compute integrals or combinatorial probabilities, then sum the resulting series; illustrate interchange of sum and expectation when justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert combinatorial probabilities to integrals and factorial expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent probabilities of order-statistic-type events by integrals over t and use factorial expressions, e.g., (i−1)! / i! factors, leading to series summable to expressions involving e^{1/2} (A4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the integral representation and simplify using Beta/Gamma factorial identities; sum termwise using known series expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define optimal-play recursions and prove by induction in combinatorial games
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce functions a(n), b(n) for optimal scores when a player moves first, derive recurrence relations (e.g., a(n)=a(n−7)+1), prove base cases and inductive step to obtain closed values (A5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish base cases explicitly, argue monotonicity/inequalities from game properties, reduce general n to smaller n via splitting strategies and worst-case responses, and complete induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce impartial game positions to sums of independent subgames
rubrics_metrics.description: When a move splits position into intervals, analyze resulting components independently and combine optimal play outcomes via min/max formulas (A5: use splitting into intervals of lengths i and n−2−i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model splitting as independent subgames, use optimal-response reasoning (player chooses which subgame to play) and pass-option arguments as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct special point configurations (cosines) to attain extremal moment conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose x_j = cos(...) so that sums of odd powers vanish up to a given order, producing extremal examples (A6 explicit cosine construction to show m≥n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit trigonometric choices and justify inequalities (e.g., ordering −1<x1<...<x_{2n}<1) and algebraic identities linking power sums to roots of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove equality of multisets from equality of odd power sums via rational/power-series methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Form rational functions f(z)=∑ x_i z/(1−x_i^2 z^2) and equate power series expansions to deduce multisets coincide (A6 lemma: matching odd power sums implies multisets equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue about poles and residues to recover each x_i and multiplicity; use uniqueness of pole-residue data or invertibility of Vandermonde matrices as alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Newton (Girard–Newton) identities and parity of symmetric functions to reach contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate vanishing of power sums into vanishing of odd elementary symmetric functions and deduce polynomial parity properties that lead to contradictions (A6 second solution: odd polynomial implication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Newton identities relating power sums to elementary symmetric functions, then show the algebraic implications for polynomial structure and roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the implicit function theorem to deform degenerate solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Start from a degenerate solution and use the implicit function theorem and nonvanishing Jacobian minors to produce nearby nondegenerate solutions (A6 remark/implicit deformation argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify Jacobian matrix and show maximal minors nonzero (e.g., scaled Vandermonde), normalize parameters, and explain how small perturbation yields desired configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal power-series/group structure to deduce integrality and parity properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Work in ring of exponential generating functions and subgroup structure (G and H) to deduce properties like k! b_k being odd (B1 second solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express e^{P(x)} as product involving series in subgroup H; track 2-adic divisibility through factorials and subgroup membership to conclude parity facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial exponential formula and involution to determine parity of coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret coefficients as weighted counts over set partitions and employ an involution to cancel pairs leaving parity determined by fixed points (B1 third solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe combinatorial model (colorings/part sizes), define involution with no fixed points on nontrivial set, and conclude parity from fixed-point count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use closure properties (cross product, orthogonality, norms) to classify finite algebraic/geometric sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage closure under cross product and norm-multiplicativity to show all nonzero vectors must be unit vectors and S must be {0, ±v1, ±v2, ±v3} (B2 classification of possible sizes 1 or 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue by contradiction using norm growth under repeated cross products, show orthogonality relations force an orthonormal basis, and enumerate all elements produced by cross products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagate colorings or labels via multiplicative/additive relations to show rapid closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how colors evolve under given operations (doubling, adding fractions) and deduce eventual homogenization (B3: show R2=R+).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find small-step implications (if y∈B1 then y/2∈R1), assume contrary configuration and derive contradictions by tracking forced colors of related numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modular residue arguments to restrict lengths of sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue residues modulo small integers (mod 3) force constraints on possible sequences of arithmetic progressions, restricting n to multiples of 3 (B4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce by scaling to integer differences, analyze residues of consecutive triples, and deduce divisibility constraints on total length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct sequences by concatenating arithmetic progressions with disjoint residue classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Build long examples by concatenating progressions designed to occupy disjoint residue classes (B4 explicit construction for n multiples of 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify component progressions with complementary mod patterns (odds, multiples of 4, etc.) and check pairwise distinctness by residue analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude small exceptional cases by finite casework after normalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Normalize smallest difference to 1 and exhaustively check small possibilities by shifting/scaling to rule out small n (B4 shows n=6 impossible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rescale and shift to reduce to a finite list of candidate patterns and check each for failure to meet required arithmetic progression property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce counterexamples for necessity and use generating-function factorization for sufficiency in probability inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Show p>1/4 fails via explicit sequences (B5), then translate probability mass into polynomial coefficients and factor as g(x)g(x^{-1}) to compare coefficients for sufficiency when p≤1/4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute explicit probabilities for well-chosen sequences to show contradiction for p>1/4; for sufficiency factor the generating polynomial and compare symmetric coefficients using Cauchy-type inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use characteristic functions (Fourier transforms) to bound point probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent discrete distributions via characteristic functions, note nonnegativity of transform implies P(S=b)≤P(S=0), and apply to product of independent variables (B5 second solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish ϕ_X(θ) ≥ 0 for building-block variables, multiply transforms for sums, and use inversion integral to compare probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze functional equations via limits, limsup/liminf, and monotonicity to classify solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Study behavior as x→0+ and x→∞ to deduce limit values, show x f(x)→0 near 0, deduce monotonicity and symmetry (f(1/y)+f(y)=1), then solve to obtain parametric family f(x)=1/(1+cx) (B6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use substitutions into the functional equation, derive inequalities linking limsup/liminf, prove monotonicity by contradiction and continuity, use scaling invariance to normalize, and solve for parameter c≥0.
